Safe Haven or Tax Haven? The Rise of South Africans on the Isle of Man

By: Nickolaus Bauer | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A a new migration trend is quietly taking root — and SARS is struggling to keep up. The Isle of Man, a rainy, wind-battered Crown Dependency in the Irish Sea, is fast becoming a preferred destinatio

Unique Selling Point:
This story unpacks the rise of this unique offshore community, explores the implications for SARS and the national tax base, and investigates whether the South African government has the will or the resources to prevent mass base erosion and profit shifting.


Summary:
The Isle of Man is fast becoming one of the world’s most rapidly growing enclaves of South African expatriates — a scenic outpost with zero capital gains tax, no inheritance tax, and low corporate rates. While most South Africans here speak of quality of life and safety as primary reasons for leaving, experts warn that the exodus — especially of high earners — is a clear signal of eroding confidence in South Africa’s fiscal future.
But it’s not just fear — it’s strategy. More and more South Africans are looking to keep their options open and safeguard their wealth by parking assets offshore, setting up trusts, or restructuring businesses via jurisdictions like the Isle of Man. What began as financial emigration has now evolved into a well-oiled playbook for tax-efficient living abroad.


Further information:
Protagonists:
Rich Mulholland – Entrepreneur and international speaker
Roelf Odendaal – Turnstone Group
Vanessa Naude – IOM Relocate
Chanelle Sukhoo – Journalist, Manx Radio
Edward Kieswetter – SARS Commissioner
Johann van Loggerenberg – Former SARS forensic investigator
Key Themes:
The Push Factors:
Declining service delivery and growing distrust in South African governance
National uncertainty over looming tax hikes and fiscal crises
Concerns about proposed changes to capital gains and inheritance tax
Weakening currency and fears around exchange control tightening
Rising cost of compliance and aggressive SARS auditing
Declining faith in political and economic stability
Isle of Man’s zero capital gains and inheritance taxes
Strong regulatory environment, privacy protections, and low crime
High-end financial planning and corporate structuring services
Visa routes for entrepreneurs, high-net-worth individuals, and remote workers
The Pull Factors:
Isle of Man offers low taxes, high safety, and a pro-business environment
South African expats report stronger community bonds and quality of life
Established infrastructure for setting up trusts, companies, and residency
The Impact on South Africa:
Erosion of the country’s domestic tax base
Growing inequality between those who can afford to leave and those who can’t
“Brain drain” and capital flight accelerating amid lack of policy response
The Manx Perspective:
A vibrant and growing South African community, complete with festivals and expat meetups
A local economy benefiting from highly skilled immigrants
Questions about the Isle of Man’s role in facilitating global tax avoidance


Visual Approach:
Contrast: Sweeping drone shots of the idyllic Isle of Man countryside and new South African homes, contrasted with images of decaying infrastructure and loadshedding in South Africa.
Community Moments: Footage from the recent South African Festival on the Isle, and scenes from the “Isle of Man Indaba” held in SA encouraging others to emigrate.
Expert Testimony: Interviews with tax experts and former SARS investigators, cleanly framed and factually grounded.
Data Visualization: Infographics illustrating base erosion and profit shifting (BEPS) and the outflow of South African capital.
Emotional Weight: Testimonials from South Africans who feel deeply conflicted about leaving.

Draft script:
Scene 1: Introduction – A Tale of Two Countries
Location: Aerial shots of the Isle of Man coastline — green hills, sleek harbourside homes, happy families at play.
Cut to: congested SA cities, potholes, queues at Home Affairs, candlelit dinner tables under loadshedding.
Nickolaus Bauer (PTC):
“Some call it a tax haven. Others, a safe haven. The Isle of Man — a tiny British Crown dependency in the Irish Sea — is quietly becoming home to thousands of South Africans looking for stability, security, and a new start.”
VO:
“From entrepreneurs and investors to young families and retirees, this island is now hosting a fast-growing community of South Africans. But what does their departure say about South Africa’s future — and who’s watching where their money goes?”
Visual cue: Rich Mulholland jogging, Roelf Odendaal at his desk overlooking the sea, Vanessa Naude fielding relocation calls, Chanelle Sukhoo reading Manx Radio bulletins.

Scene 2: Rich Mulholland’s Story – Escaping the Noise
Location: Rich’s contemporary coastal home, overlooking the sea.
Visuals: Rich on a call with clients in SA, his kids biking freely, his bookshelf stacked with leadership books.
VO:
“Entrepreneur and speaker Rich Mulholland moved to the Isle of Man not to disappear, but to live deliberately. For him, it wasn’t about dodging taxes — it was about dignity.”
Rich Mulholland:
“I didn’t come here to avoid paying tax. I came because I want a place where my kids can grow up without hearing a generator every night, where I can build without constant fear of policy collapse.”
Cutaway:
Rich co-hosting a webinar with a South African team, showing continuity of engagement.
Rich (cont’d):
“My business still operates in South Africa. I love the country. But you get to a point where optimism starts to feel irresponsible.”

Scene 3: The Community Boom – New Roots on Old Shores
Location: South African Festival on the Isle, drone flyover with visuals of South African shops, biltong butchers, and café meetups.
VO:
“Far from hiding in secrecy, the South Africans here have created something unique: a vibrant, visible community. They’ve held festivals, launched businesses, and even hosted a Manx Indaba in Johannesburg encouraging others to consider the move.”
Vanessa Naude (IOM Relocate):
“We’re not talking about dodgy shell companies. These are families, professionals, retirees. They’re coming here with skills, wealth, and heart — and they’re building lives.”
Visuals:
Vanessa walking a couple through their new home, explaining tax residency. Montage of kids at school, people at church, and expats gathering for a community braai.
Chanelle Sukhoo (Manx Radio):
“There’s a real pride here. South Africans on the Isle aren’t invisible — they’re forming a cultural thread in the fabric of Manx life.”

Scene 4: Building a Tax-Efficient Life
Location: Interview with Roelf Odendaal, Turnstone Group offices
VO:
“Roelf Odendaal helps South Africans navigate this new offshore frontier. His company, Turnstone, specializes in corporate structuring, asset migration, and residency planning.”
Roelf Odendaal:
“It’s not about evading tax. It’s about optimizing what’s legal — and protecting wealth against the unpredictability back home.”
Visuals: Roelf video conferencing with clients in Cape Town; a diagram showing common structuring routes (trusts, IP holdings, etc.)
VO:
“Roelf sees a new kind of emigration: not necessarily physical, but financial — with roots in deepening distrust of the South African state.”

Scene 5: The Bigger Picture – Tax Avoidance vs. Evasion
Location: Dimly lit archive-style set with SARS documents, diagrams, headlines.
VO:
“Yet behind the warmth and wine lies a deeper concern — the line between legitimate tax planning and aggressive avoidance.”
Johann van Loggerenberg:
“Base erosion and profit shifting isn’t illegal per se. But it's highly problematic. It’s a legal stretch that weakens our ability to collect revenue for basic services. And the fact is: SARS just does not have the skills or resources to tackle this.”
Graphics:
Money flowing from Johannesburg to the Isle, animation of trust structures and IP havens.
Cut to: Old SARS tax audit notices, followed by glossy marketing from offshore firms.

Scene 6: What SARS Is Facing – Under Siege
Location: SARS HQ, Pretoria – sterile, tense. Kieswetter in interview setup with financial charts in background.
Edward Kieswetter (SARS Commissioner):
“We are acutely aware of the risks posed by aggressive tax planning strategies. But our capacity is stretched. We’re not just fighting criminals — we’re up against billion-dollar advisory firms.”
VO:
“South Africa's tax base is shrinking, even as the state debates raising VAT. And SARS insiders admit they’re outgunned when it comes to high-net-worth individuals relocating assets offshore.”
Cut to: Kieswetter with staff in a tax compliance strategy meeting; over-the-shoulder shot of leaked emails about trust structures.

Scene 7: A Country on the Brink – Voting with Their Feet
Location: Parliamentary chambers, protest marches, pensioners in food queues, families flying out at OR Tambo.
VO:
“As South Africa teeters on the brink of a fiscal reckoning, citizens are voting with their feet and their funds. The middle and upper class is exiting — not just physically, but financially.”
Nickolaus Bauer (PTC):
“Some go for safety. Others for schooling. Many for stability. But behind each departure is a deeper message: people are losing faith in the South African state.”
Cut to:
Edward Kieswetter watching a presentation on capital flight. Vanessa on a Zoom call guiding a family through the move. Rich packing a care package for relatives in SA.

Scene 8: Conclusion – Diaspora or Departure?
Location: Split screen: Roelf Odendaal managing logistics at Turnstone Group on the Isle vs. clips of Johannesburg traffic and failing streetlights.
VO:
“Whether it’s brain drain or capital flight, South Africa’s loss is the Isle of Man’s gain. But experts say there’s an opportunity in the diaspora — if it’s engaged meaningfully.”
Roelf Odendaal (Turnstone Group):
“We’re still South African. We haven’t given up. But we need a government that makes it easy to stay — or at least, hard to leave.”
Chanelle Sukhoo:
“This island has given people a second chapter. But it doesn’t mean they’ve closed the book on South Africa.”
Nickolaus Bauer (PTC):
“From the windswept cliffs of the Isle of Man to the power-starved homes of South Africa, a quiet exodus is gathering pace. The question isn’t who’s leaving. It’s why — and what can be done to stop the bleeding. “In the end, this isn’t just about tax. It’s about trust. And if that’s broken, no policy will be strong enough to hold the line. South Africans aren’t disappearing. They’re just starting to build — somewhere else.”
Final montage:
South Africans gathered at a cliffside picnic on the Isle, laughing with family, a child flying a kite bearing the SA flag — slowly fading into a Johannesburg sunset flickering during loadshedding.

Press Release:


Safe Haven or Tax Haven?
The Isle of Man: it’s home to one of the world’s most rapidly growing populations of South African expatriates. Fear of crime and economic collapse may drive many to its rocky shores, but its growing Saffer community is just as motivated by the opportunity for “tax efficient” living. The island is a scenic outpost with zero capital gains tax, no inheritance tax, and low corporate rates. As confidence in South Africa’s economy continues to crumble and emigration erodes the tiny tax-paying public, what are the consequences for inequality, service delivery and social stability back home?
Producer & Presenter: Nickolaus Bauer

Script:



VO: It’s been another busy, often confusing, week on the South African news front. Right now, it seems our politics, economy and social cohesion are in turmoil. It’s an environment in which some contemplate moving to other parts of the world, a decision thousands have already made. (MONTAGE – FAST PACED SOME OF THE WEEK’S MAIN NEWS EVENTS).


But how many would consider a life on a rainy windswept island at the mercy of the stormy Atlantic Ocean? Well, quite a few, it turns out. (VISUALS OF LANDSCAPE IN ISLE OF MAN)


LINK: Here we are nestled between Belfast and Liverpool in the middle of the Irish Sea. The Isle of Man is a European financial hub for multinational corporations and wealthy individuals. And is home to one of the fastest growing South African expat communities.

VO: South African emigration isn’t unusual, but this place is about as removed from the vibrancy of London or the outdoor lifestyle of Perth as you’re likely to get. (VISUALS OF LIFE IN ISLE OF MAN)

The Isle of Man, what’s known as a self-governing British crown dependency, is sandwiched between the UK and Ireland. (VISUALS OF LIFE IN ISLE OF MAN)
It has a rugged coastline, medieval castles, a rural landscape… and is home to a surprising number of South Africans. (VISUALS OF LANDSCAPE IN ISLE OF MAN)
Of a population of just over 84 thousand, ten percent are Saffers, (SOUTH AFRICA FESTIVAL)
making them the island’s biggest ethnic minority. (RICH ON HIS TREADMILL)

RICH MULHOLLAND, MISSING LINK
“One worry that I had is if the rand continued to perform worse against international currencies, then I would be a prisoner of economy and with, you know, ten, 15 good working years ahead of me and left. I thought, how do I build myself up to have an international wealth relevance. And I guess I just felt that if I wanted to generate that wealth in South Africa, it would mean me turning up the dial past a level that I didn't necessarily want.”



VO: Media and Communications entrepreneur, Rich Mullholland, moved here last year. He’s maintaining his South African businesses, but, like many South Africans, he found the draw of doing business in Pounds difficult to resist. (RICH IN HIS OFFICE THEN A WIDE OF US IN CONVERSATION)

RICH MULHOLLAND, MISSING LINK
“I’ve played a hedge. So I'm hedging against the fact that I'm building up international client base and international work and a small entity here. But my primary entity is in South Africa, where we make most of our money anyway.”


UPSOUND RADIO STATION

CHANNELLE SUKHOO, MANX RADIO
“It is very safe. It's one of the safest places I've ever lived in or ever been in.

VO: Channele Sukhoo, from Durban, moved here in 2021. With a background in media she found work at a local radio station. Not a financially-minded businessperson like Rich, she moved to the Isle of Man for very different reasons. (WALKING THROUGH THE RADIO STATION WITH ME)

CHANNELLE SUKHOO
It allows you space to focus on other things you're not worried about. Oh, do I need to get home and charge my phone or charge my computers? Do we have watches in the taps? Do I need to fill up a bucket quickly? You know, it's those stresses that you don't have to think about.

MORE RADIO UPSOUND

CHANELLE SUKHOO, MANX RADIO
If someone loses the money or leave the money at the ATM, someone else will post on Facebook. I found £100 at the ATM. At this time, on this day at this location, and they wouldn't look for you to return it.”


LINK PTC:

This is something of a vanishing site in South Africa. People out in the evening without a care in the world for their safety. This may just be the non-financial security offered by the Isle of Man that makes it so attractive to South Africans.

The Isle of Man has one of the lowest crime rates in Europe, with violent crime virtually unheard of and petty crime extremely rare. (OKES CHILLING IN THE SQUARE AND KIDS PLAYING )


BOEREWORS UPSOUND

VO: As for those South African expats not quite able to fully cut ties with home, the Isle of Man has them covered, too. (PRODUCTS SIGN AND PRICES)

LINK: With all of these South African products, this supermarket could easily be found back home. But the prices are in pounds and there’s more than enough South Africans here to keep demand for these lekker goodies going strong.



VISUAL PAUSE - WALKING WITH ROELF

NICKOLAUS
It is quite beautiful even though it is so wet…

ROELF ODENDAAL, ISLE OF MAN INDABA
It is a beautiful place and life is good. The quality of life is good…

VO: Roelf Odendaal is from Potchefstroom. Having moved here almost 25 years ago he’s among the more settled of the SA expats. (US TALKING SHIT NEXT TO THE DOCKS)

ROELF ODENDAAL, ISLE OF MAN INDABA
From a business point of view… It’s an entrepreneurial island.

VO: Roelf started what he called the Isle of Man Indaba in 2019. Its an annual roadshow that attracts other South Africans to the island by showcasing the benefits of international business expansion, wealth management, and asset protection on the Island. (ISLE OF MAN INDABA PICS)

ROELF ODENDAAL
There’s opportunities you can seize by being here. We are a tax neutral jurisdiction and that is a financial benefit.

VO: A tax neutral jurisdiction is a place where income, capital, or assets can be held or moved without triggering additional layers of tax—meaning it doesn’t add any extra tax on top of what’s already owed in your home country. (US TALKING SHIT NEXT TO THE DOCKS)

People here also pay no or very low rates of tax. Income is taxed at a maximum of 22 percent, there’s no capital gains tax payable if you sell a property or shares, businesses pay no corporate tax, and there’s no inheritance tax. Tax Haven? More like tax heaven. (FLAGS AND THOSE GOEDERS)

ROELF ODENDAAL
“You may have the benefit of a tax saving living here. But life on the Isle of Man is still in pounds. Its still expensive from a South African point of view to live here.”

UPSOUND TRANSITION INTO THE MOTOR RACE

VO: Each year, the Island hosts what’s known as the Tourist Trophy or motorcycle TT. It’s a high-octane international race held on the island’s normally quiet country roads. To date, more than 270 racers have lost their lives here. (MOTOR RACE)

To many, it’s as out of place on a rural island in the middle of the Irish Sea as, say, more than 8 thousand South Africans. (PEOPLE AND LANDASCAPE)

JOHANN VAN LOGGERENBERG, FORMER SARS FORENSIC INVESTIGATOR
“You’re going to look for those places in the world where there is a mix of safety and a mix of benefit.”

VO: Johann Van Loggerenberg is a former South African Revenue Service forensic investigator. He believes the Isle of Man attracting South Africans looking to get bang for their buck is a no brainer. (CUTAWAY OF ME IN FRONT OF A COMPUTER)

JOHANN VAN LOGGERENBERG, FORMER SARS FORENSIC INVESTIGATOR
“Certainly people who are able to do so will look to optimise their money or put it into places where it can grow quicker and faster and so on. That's just a natural consequence of globalisation.”

VO: So, while the Isle of Man certainly has its attractions, it seems its approach to tax is one of its biggest pull factors. And that’s put it and the South Africans who move there in the crosshairs of SARS. Who have promised to clamp down on anyone looking to emigrate without paying their fair share of tax(SARS CUTAWAYS)

EDWARD KIESWETTER, SARS COMMISSIONER
“There are many, many millions of outstanding returns collectively that present an opportunity for us to go and fetch the money that is already due to the state.”

NICKOLAUS BAUER
Would you say it's a complete myth, that a place like the Isle of Man is a tax haven?

ROELF ODENDAAL, ISLE OF MAN INDABA
I would absolutely say its a myth. It's not something that drives the Isle of Man economy. It's not something that the Isle of Man pushes. It's something that is there to be used. But it's not a driver in the Isle of Man. And therefore the word tax haven for me is a four letter word. It doesn't describe what the Isle of Man is.

RICH MULHOLLAND, MISSING LINK
“Anybody who thinks you're moving to Isle of Man to save money in tax, maybe billionaires, but any average person, this is not the reason you move here.The weeks before we left South Africa, my tax immigration status was in. I paid my exit fee. So I worked everything out. I paid that and I left. I wanted to make sure that this was not murky waters.”


VO: And as the South African diaspora continues to grow… What lessons can be learnedfrom the South Africans who’ve moved here? (RICH AND I WALKING ON THE PROMENADE)

RICH MULHOLLAND, MISSING LINK

“South Africans are in pretty high demand. We're a pretty good quality export. So moving to a different economy, evangelising and becoming a diplomat for this South African way of thinking is, is how I see what's happened. And I would argue that this island anyway, and the world at large embrace the South Africans in that regard.”
PROMO 1
VO: They’re leaving in droves…
SOT (Rich Mulholland): “My company, my staff, my my means. It comes from South Africa. I'm still in South Africa.”
VO: But what makes this remote, windswept place such a magnet for South Africans?
SOT (Roelf Odendaal): “We are a tax neutral jurisdiction… and that is a financial benefit.”
VO: From tax breaks to safety… Why thousands are trading South Africa for a tiny island in the Irish Sea.


PROMO 2
VO: Is the Isle of Man be the escape many South Africans have been waiting for?
SOT (Channele Sukhoo): “Those stresses that you you don't have to think about. You know, you can focus on other stuff.…”
VO: But is the Isle of Man a secure paradise — or a tax haven with a price?
SOT (Roelf Odendaal): “It only means you are managing the taxation of your international organisations in a much more efficient way”



PROMO 3
VO: A bolthole for the country’s talent
SOT (Rich Mulholland): “I'm driving South African entrepreneurship in an international economy.”
VO: Carte Blanche visits the Isle of Man — where thousands South Africans are putting down new roots…
VO: But is SARS watching?
SOT (Roelf Odendaal): “Because you are trading through the Isle of Man doesn't mean you are suddenly tax free.”



PROMO 4
VO: It’s quiet, it's cold… and it's calling thousands of South Africans.
SOT (Roelf Odendaal): “It’s an entrepreneurial island.”
VO: But behind the stunning scenery lies a different kind of attraction —
VO: Pounds, perks… and pressure from SARS.
SOT (Nickolaus Bauer): “Would you say it’s a complete myth that the Isle of Man is a tax haven?”

Montage of kids at school, people at church, and expats gathering for a community braai. Chanelle Sukhoo (Manx Radio): “There’s a real pride here. South Africans on the Isle aren’t invisible — they’re forming a cultural thread in the fabric of Manx life.” Scene 4: Building a Tax-Efficient Life Location: Interview with Roelf Odendaal, Turnstone Group offices VO: “Roelf Odendaal helps South Africans navigate this new offshore frontier. His company, Turnstone, specializes in corporate structuring, asset migration, and residency planning.” Roelf Odendaal: “It’s not about evading tax. It’s about optimizing what’s legal — and protecting wealth against the unpredictability back home.” Visuals: Roelf video conferencing with clients in Cape Town; a diagram showing common structuring routes (trusts, IP holdings, etc.) VO: “Roelf sees a new kind of emigration: not necessarily physical, but financial — with roots in deepening distrust of the South African state.” Scene 5: The Bigger Picture – Tax Avoidance vs. Evasion Location: Dimly lit archive-style set with SARS documents, diagrams, headlines. VO: “Yet behind the warmth and wine lies a deeper concern — the line between legitimate tax planning and aggressive avoidance.” Johann van Loggerenberg: “Base erosion and profit shifting isn’t illegal per se. But it's highly problematic. It’s a legal stretch that weakens our ability to collect revenue for basic services. And the fact is: SARS just does not have the skills or resources to tackle this.” Graphics: Money flowing from Johannesburg to the Isle, animation of trust structures and IP havens. Cut to: Old SARS tax audit notices, followed by glossy marketing from offshore firms. Scene 6: What SARS Is Facing – Under Siege Location: SARS HQ, Pretoria – sterile, tense. Kieswetter in interview setup with financial charts in background. Edward Kieswetter (SARS Commissioner): “We are acutely aware of the risks posed by aggressive tax planning strategies. But our capacity is stretched. We’re not just fighting criminals — we’re up against billion-dollar advisory firms.” VO: “South Africa's tax base is shrinking, even as the state debates raising VAT. And SARS insiders admit they’re outgunned when it comes to high-net-worth individuals relocating assets offshore.” Cut to: Kieswetter with staff in a tax compliance strategy meeting; over-the-shoulder shot of leaked emails about trust structures. Scene 7: A Country on the Brink – Voting with Their Feet Location: Parliamentary chambers, protest marches, pensioners in food queues, families flying out at OR Tambo. VO: “As South Africa teeters on the brink of a fiscal reckoning, citizens are voting with their feet and their funds. 2025 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Press Release: Safe Haven or Tax Haven? The Isle of Man: it’s home to one of the world’s most rapidly growing populations of South African expatriates. Fear of crime and economic collapse may drive many to its rocky shores, but its growing Saffer community is just as motivated by the opportunity for “tax efficient” living. The island is a scenic outpost with zero capital gains tax, no inheritance tax, and low corporate rates. As confidence in South Africa’s economy continues to crumble and emigration erodes the tiny tax-paying public, what are the consequences for inequality, service delivery and social stability back home? Producer & Presenter: Nickolaus Bauer Script: VO: It’s been another busy, often confusing, week on the South African news front. Right now, it seems our politics, economy and social cohesion are in turmoil. It’s an environment in which some contemplate moving to other parts of the world, a decision thousands have already made. (MONTAGE – FAST PACED SOME OF THE WEEK’S MAIN NEWS EVENTS). But how many would consider a life on a rainy windswept island at the mercy of the stormy Atlantic Ocean? Well, quite a few, it turns out. (VISUALS OF LANDSCAPE IN ISLE OF MAN) LINK: Here we are nestled between Belfast and Liverpool in the middle of the Irish Sea. The Isle of Man is a European financial hub for multinational corporations and wealthy individuals. And is home to one of the fastest growing South African expat communities. VO: South African emigration isn’t unusual, but this place is about as removed from the vibrancy of London or the outdoor lifestyle of Perth as you’re likely to get. (VISUALS OF LIFE IN ISLE OF MAN) The Isle of Man, what’s known as a self-governing British crown dependency, is sandwiched between the UK and Ireland. (VISUALS OF LIFE IN ISLE OF MAN) It has a rugged coastline, medieval castles, a rural landscape… and is home to a surprising number of South Africans. (VISUALS OF LANDSCAPE IN ISLE OF MAN) Of a population of just over 84 thousand, ten percent are Saffers, (SOUTH AFRICA FESTIVAL) making them the island’s biggest ethnic minority. (RICH ON HIS TREADMILL) RICH MULHOLLAND, MISSING LINK “One worry that I had is if the rand continued to perform worse against international currencies, then I would be a prisoner of economy and with, you know, ten, 15 good working years ahead of me and left. I thought, how do I build myself up to have an international wealth relevance. And I guess I just felt that if I wanted to generate that wealth in South Africa, it would mean me turning up the dial past a level that I didn't necessarily want.” VO: Media and Communications entrepreneur, Rich Mullholland, moved here last year. He’s maintaining his South African businesses, but, like many South Africans, he found the draw of doing business in Pounds difficult to resist. (RICH IN HIS OFFICE THEN A WIDE OF US IN CONVERSATION) RICH MULHOLLAND, MISSING LINK “I’ve played a hedge. So I'm hedging against the fact that I'm building up international client base and international work and a small entity here. But my primary entity is in South Africa, where we make most of our money anyway.” UPSOUND RADIO STATION CHANNELLE SUKHOO, MANX RADIO “It is very safe. It's one of the safest places I've ever lived in or ever been in. VO: Channele Sukhoo, from Durban, moved here in 2021. With a background in media she found work at a local radio station. Not a financially-minded businessperson like Rich, she moved to the Isle of Man for very different reasons. (WALKING THROUGH THE RADIO STATION WITH ME) CHANNELLE SUKHOO It allows you space to focus on other things you're not worried about. Oh, do I need to get home and charge my phone or charge my computers? Do we have watches in the taps? Do I need to fill up a bucket quickly? You know, it's those stresses that you don't have to think about. MORE RADIO UPSOUND CHANELLE SUKHOO, MANX RADIO If someone loses the money or leave the money at the ATM, someone else will post on Facebook. I found £100 at the ATM. At this time, on this day at this location, and they wouldn't look for you to return it.” LINK PTC: This is something of a vanishing site in South Africa. People out in the evening without a care in the world for their safety. This may just be the non-financial security offered by the Isle of Man that makes it so attractive to South Africans. The Isle of Man has one of the lowest crime rates in Europe, with violent crime virtually unheard of and petty crime extremely rare. (OKES CHILLING IN THE SQUARE AND KIDS PLAYING ) BOEREWORS UPSOUND VO: As for those South African expats not quite able to fully cut ties with home, the Isle of Man has them covered, too. (PRODUCTS SIGN AND PRICES) LINK: With all of these South African products, this supermarket could easily be found back home. But the prices are in pounds and there’s more than enough South Africans here to keep demand for these lekker goodies going strong. VISUAL PAUSE - WALKING WITH ROELF NICKOLAUS It is quite beautiful even though it is so wet… ROELF ODENDAAL, ISLE OF MAN INDABA It is a beautiful place and life is good. The quality of life is good… VO: Roelf Odendaal is from Potchefstroom. Having moved here almost 25 years ago he’s among the more settled of the SA expats. (US TALKING SHIT NEXT TO THE DOCKS) ROELF ODENDAAL, ISLE OF MAN INDABA From a business point of view… It’s an entrepreneurial island. VO: Roelf started what he called the Isle of Man Indaba in 2019. Its an annual roadshow that attracts other South Africans to the island by showcasing the benefits of international business expansion, wealth management, and asset protection on the Island. (ISLE OF MAN INDABA PICS) ROELF ODENDAAL There’s opportunities you can seize by being here. We are a tax neutral jurisdiction and that is a financial benefit. VO: A tax neutral jurisdiction is a place where income, capital, or assets can be held or moved without triggering additional layers of tax—meaning it doesn’t add any extra tax on top of what’s already owed in your home country. (US TALKING SHIT NEXT TO THE DOCKS) People here also pay no or very low rates of tax. Income is taxed at a maximum of 22 percent, there’s no capital gains tax payable if you sell a property or shares, businesses pay no corporate tax, and there’s no inheritance tax. Tax Haven? More like tax heaven. (FLAGS AND THOSE GOEDERS) ROELF ODENDAAL “You may have the benefit of a tax saving living here. But life on the Isle of Man is still in pounds. Its still expensive from a South African point of view to live here.” UPSOUND TRANSITION INTO THE MOTOR RACE VO: Each year, the Island hosts what’s known as the Tourist Trophy or motorcycle TT. It’s a high-octane international race held on the island’s normally quiet country roads. To date, more than 270 racers have lost their lives here. (MOTOR RACE) To many, it’s as out of place on a rural island in the middle of the Irish Sea as, say, more than 8 thousand South Africans. (PEOPLE AND LANDASCAPE) JOHANN VAN LOGGERENBERG, FORMER SARS FORENSIC INVESTIGATOR “You’re going to look for those places in the world where there is a mix of safety and a mix of benefit.” VO: Johann Van Loggerenberg is a former South African Revenue Service forensic investigator. He believes the Isle of Man attracting South Africans looking to get bang for their buck is a no brainer. (CUTAWAY OF ME IN FRONT OF A COMPUTER) JOHANN VAN LOGGERENBERG, FORMER SARS FORENSIC INVESTIGATOR “Certainly people who are able to do so will look to optimise their money or put it into places where it can grow quicker and faster and so on. That's just a natural consequence of globalisation.” VO: So, while the Isle of Man certainly has its attractions, it seems its approach to tax is one of its biggest pull factors. And that’s put it and the South Africans who move there in the crosshairs of SARS. Who have promised to clamp down on anyone looking to emigrate without paying their fair share of tax(SARS CUTAWAYS) EDWARD KIESWETTER, SARS COMMISSIONER “There are many, many millions of outstanding returns collectively that present an opportunity for us to go and fetch the money that is already due to the state.” NICKOLAUS BAUER Would you say it's a complete myth, that a place like the Isle of Man is a tax haven? ROELF ODENDAAL, ISLE OF MAN INDABA I would absolutely say its a myth. It's not something that drives the Isle of Man economy. It's not something that the Isle of Man pushes. It's something that is there to be used. But it's not a driver in the Isle of Man. And therefore the word tax haven for me is a four letter word. It doesn't describe what the Isle of Man is. RICH MULHOLLAND, MISSING LINK “Anybody who thinks you're moving to Isle of Man to save money in tax, maybe billionaires, but any average person, this is not the reason you move here.The weeks before we left South Africa, my tax immigration status was in. I paid my exit fee. So I worked everything out. I paid that and I left. I wanted to make sure that this was not murky waters.” VO: And as the South African diaspora continues to grow… What lessons can be learnedfrom the South Africans who’ve moved here? (RICH AND I WALKING ON THE PROMENADE) RICH MULHOLLAND, MISSING LINK “South Africans are in pretty high demand. We're a pretty good quality export. So moving to a different economy, evangelising and becoming a diplomat for this South African way of thinking is, is how I see what's happened. And I would argue that this island anyway, and the world at large embrace the South Africans in that regard.” PROMO 1 VO: They’re leaving in droves… SOT (Rich Mulholland): “My company, my staff, my my means. It comes from South Africa. I'm still in South Africa.” VO: But what makes this remote, windswept place such a magnet for South Africans? SOT (Roelf Odendaal): “We are a tax neutral jurisdiction… and that is a financial benefit.” VO: From tax breaks to safety… Why thousands are trading South Africa for a tiny island in the Irish Sea. PROMO 2 VO: Is the Isle of Man be the escape many South Africans have been waiting for? SOT (Channele Sukhoo): “Those stresses that you you don't have to think about. You know, you can focus on other stuff.…” VO: But is the Isle of Man a secure paradise — or a tax haven with a price? SOT (Roelf Odendaal): “It only means you are managing the taxation of your international organisations in a much more efficient way” PROMO 3 VO: A bolthole for the country’s talent SOT (Rich Mulholland): “I'm driving South African entrepreneurship in an international economy.” VO: Carte Blanche visits the Isle of Man — where thousands South Africans are putting down new roots… VO: But is SARS watching? SOT (Roelf Odendaal): “Because you are trading through the Isle of Man doesn't mean you are suddenly tax free.” PROMO 4 VO: It’s quiet, it's cold… and it's calling thousands of South Africans. SOT (Roelf Odendaal): “It’s an entrepreneurial island.” VO: But behind the stunning scenery lies a different kind of attraction — VO: Pounds, perks… and pressure from SARS. SOT (Nickolaus Bauer): “Would you say it’s a complete myth that the Isle of Man is a tax haven?”

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A a new migration trend is quietly taking root — and SARS is struggling to keep up. The Isle of Man, a rainy, wind-battered Crown Dependency in the Irish Sea, is fast becoming a preferred destinatio
metadata.Unique Selling Point: This story unpacks the rise of this unique offshore community, explores the implications for SARS and the national tax base, and investigates whether the South African government has the will or the resources to prevent mass base erosion and profit shifting.
metadata.Summary: The Isle of Man is fast becoming one of the world’s most rapidly growing enclaves of South African expatriates — a scenic outpost with zero capital gains tax, no inheritance tax, and low corporate rates. While most South Africans here speak of quality of life and safety as primary reasons for leaving, experts warn that the exodus — especially of high earners — is a clear signal of eroding confidence in South Africa’s fiscal future. But it’s not just fear — it’s strategy. More and more South Africans are looking to keep their options open and safeguard their wealth by parking assets offshore, setting up trusts, or restructuring businesses via jurisdictions like the Isle of Man. What began as financial emigration has now evolved into a well-oiled playbook for tax-efficient living abroad.
